I'm confirming the rule: locate the 3x3 block containing yellow, then relocate its contents to the block position mirroring yellow's coordinates within its own block. Now I want to construct three more 11x11 example grids, each with a single yellow marker in different placements to test this transformation.

I need to be careful that non-grey rows and columns each contain at least one nonzero value, otherwise uniform rows of all-zero would get mistaken for grey frontier lines and corrupt the objects. So I'm designing the grids by sprinkling nonzero values throughout so every row and column outside the grey lines has enough distinct values.

Constructing test grid A...

I'm working out where the 4 sits within block(1,1), then mapping that to the corresponding target blocks in grids B and C, laying out their row values while tracking which cells are grey placeholders versus actual numbers.

Filling out the rest of the grid rows and checking each column to make sure the values don't repeat within their groups, and everything checks out.

Continuing to fill rows 9-10, then I verify all column constraints hold across every group, checking each one systematically. For a fourth pair, I decide to just reuse the original example grid rather than constructing something new, and I settle on 0 as the background color choice before submitting all four grids.
